$comment: The canonical Lamella MCP tool contract: the one source of truth for tools/list, embedded by the server rather than assembled at run time. Tool DESCRIPTIONS are AI-facing; annotations follow MCP: readOnlyHint (no side effects), destructiveHint (may overwrite / hard to undo), openWorldHint (touches external hardware). Hardware-mutating tools are gated behind the server's --allow-device flag; a read-only server still exposes compile/run/enumerate.

tools.name: lamella_check
tools.title: Check (compile only)
tools.description: Compile-CHECK a C# program WITHOUT running it -- returns the compiler's diagnostics only, or that it compiles. Fast iteration on errors before you run or deploy. A C# program binds against the corlib, which is implicit, and against the libraries it names in `references`: every other library, System.Device.Gpio among them, is a separate reference, as in a .NET project. A program using a library it does not name is refused, naming the library to add.

references.description: The libraries the program uses besides the corlib, each named as its assembly is named, such as "System.Device.Gpio". The corlib is implicit; every other library is a separate reference, as a .NET project names one. The tool's description lists the libraries this server can reference.

language.description: C#, the one language this server compiles. `lamella run <file.py>` runs a Python program on this machine.

tools.name: lamella_run
tools.title: Run (host interpreter)
tools.description: Compile and RUN a C# program on this machine's interpreter (no device needed) and return its output, its exit code, and the compiler's diagnostics. Use this to test logic quickly. A program that has not finished in 20 seconds (or the time the server was started with, --run-timeout) is stopped, and the answer says so. It runs a program against the corlib alone, so a program using a library, such as System.Device.Gpio, is refused here, naming it: lamella_check takes `references`, and lamella_run_on_device runs such a program on a board.

language.description: C#, the one language this server compiles. `lamella run <file.py>` runs a Python program on this machine.

tools.name: lamella_size
tools.title: Size report
tools.description: Bake a C# program to the flash image a board's firmware runs, without writing it, and report its size in bytes and what it carries. With `board`, the image is the one the device tools build for that board, and the answer says whether it fits the board's flash, as `lamella build <file> --board <id>` answers: lamella_fit's verdict, led by what the number leaves out (the firmware already on the board), so its headroom is an upper bound. It measures no RAM and no section sizes. A C# program binds against the corlib, which is implicit, and against the libraries it names in `references`: every other library, System.Device.Gpio among them, is a separate reference, as in a .NET project. A program using a library it does not name is refused, naming the library to add. The answer names each assembly the image carries, which build of it, and how much code it puts in the image. Without `board`, a program whose image would carry a library a chip family builds its own of, such as System.Device.Gpio, is refused: built for no board it would carry the build every family shares, which drives nothing, and on a board `new GpioController()` would throw PlatformNotSupportedException.

references.description: The libraries the program uses besides the corlib, each named as its assembly is named, such as "System.Device.Gpio". The corlib is implicit; every other library is a separate reference, as a .NET project names one. The tool's description lists the libraries this server can reference.

board.description: A board id, as lamella_boards lists them, such as "rpi-pico2-w". The image is built for that board as the device tools build it for the board that answers: it carries the board's bus table and binds its chip family's build of a library built per family. Without it the image is built for no board.

tools.name: lamella_version
tools.description: What this build IS and which agreed contracts it speaks: the tool version, the Lamella Link protocol version, the image-sidecar schema version it reads, and how many boards it carries against how many it can flash. Needs no hardware. Answer "which version is this / what does it support" FROM THIS rather than from memory -- the protocol numbers move independently of the tool version and of each other, so a tool version alone does not say what a build will accept.

tools.name: lamella_boards
tools.description: Every board this build knows, with the part it is built around and its flash and RAM budgets. Needs no hardware. The same catalog `lamella boards` lists.

tools.name: lamella_fit
tools.description: Does an image of image_bytes fit on board? Answers from the board file and the part row -- an attached board contributes nothing to the arithmetic, so this needs no hardware. The answer carries what it ASSUMED and what it cannot answer; read both. Use lamella_size to obtain image_bytes.

board.description: A board id, as lamella_boards lists it.

tools.name: lamella_reconcile
tools.description: Compare readings taken from an attached board against what that board declares it can be asked. With no readings it reports what attaching the board WOULD settle, and what nothing declared can reach.

board.description: A board id, as lamella_boards lists it.

readings.description: Discriminator name to integer value, e.g. {"chip_idcode": 195463191}.

tools.name: lamella_bake
tools.title: Bake to flash image
tools.description: Compile + BAKE a C# program into a deployable '.lmli' flash image (the on-device deploy format, carrying the corlib and the libraries the program uses) and report its size: the artifact lamella_deploy sends to a board, and what `lamella build <file> --board <id>` writes. With `board`, it is built for that board, as the device tools build it for the board that answers. To keep the image, name a NEW file with out_name: it is written in the directory the server was started with --allow-write=<dir>, never over a file already there, and a server started without that flag writes no file at all. A C# program binds against the corlib, which is implicit, and against the libraries it names in `references`: every other library, System.Device.Gpio among them, is a separate reference, as in a .NET project. A program using a library it does not name is refused, naming the library to add. The answer names each assembly the image carries, which build of it, and how much code it puts in the image. Without `board`, a program whose image would carry a library a chip family builds its own of, such as System.Device.Gpio, is refused: built for no board it would carry the build every family shares, which drives nothing, and on a board `new GpioController()` would throw PlatformNotSupportedException.

references.description: The libraries the program uses besides the corlib, each named as its assembly is named, such as "System.Device.Gpio". The corlib is implicit; every other library is a separate reference, as a .NET project names one. The tool's description lists the libraries this server can reference.

board.description: A board id, as lamella_boards lists them, such as "rpi-pico2-w". The image is built for that board as the device tools build it for the board that answers: it carries the board's bus table and binds its chip family's build of a library built per family. Without it the image is built for no board.

out_name.description: Optional: the name of a NEW file to write the image to, such as 'blink.lmli'. A plain name ending in .lmli, with no directory part. It is created in the server's --allow-write directory and never replaces a file already there.

tools.name: lamella_list_devices
tools.title: List attached boards
tools.description: Enumerate the boards attached to this machine (cross-platform) -- each entry gives its carrier (usb | serial), the target string to pass to deploy/debug tools, and its USB vid/pid/serial/product. Read-only; the first thing to call before any device action.

tools.name: lamella_identify_device
tools.title: Identify a board
tools.description: HELLO a Lamella Link target and return what it is: the board (from its product_model), its architecture and firmware build when the firmware reports them, the chip's own id under the scheme the firmware declares, the negotiated capabilities, and each resident runtime. It writes nothing to the board, though its HELLO takes the board back from a program it is running, as every tool that connects to a board does.

target.description: Where the board is: `usb`, `usb:<serial>` or `usb:<vid>:<pid>[:<serial>]` for a board's own USB, a serial port such as `COM9`, or `tcp:<host>[:<port>]` for a board on a network. lamella_list_devices lists the boards attached here and the target to give for each.

tools.name: lamella_run_on_device
tools.title: Run on a board (stored, then followed)
tools.description: Compile a C# program, store it in a board's flash over Lamella Link and run it there, then answer with what it printed and how it ended: what `lamella run <file> --device <d>` does. The board starts it without a reset, under its own scheduler, threads, locks and blocking calls included, so nothing the program prints is lost. The program is STORED: it replaces the program the board stores, and the board runs it at every reset until another is deployed. The run is followed until the program ends or the server's run timeout passes (20 seconds, or --run-timeout); a program still running then goes on running on the board, and the answer says so: the next tool that connects to the board takes it back. A board whose firmware runs a program only under the debugger is refused, naming lamella_debug_launch. A C# program binds against the corlib, which is implicit, and against the libraries it names in `references`: every other library, System.Device.Gpio among them, is a separate reference, as in a .NET project. A program using a library it does not name is refused before the board is opened, naming the library to add. The answer names each assembly the image carries, which build of it, and how much code it puts in the image. The image is built for the board that answers: it carries that board's bus table, and binds its chip family's build of a library built per family, such as System.Device.Gpio with the family's bus drivers.

target.description: Where the board is: `usb`, `usb:<serial>` or `usb:<vid>:<pid>[:<serial>]` for a board's own USB, a serial port such as `COM9`, or `tcp:<host>[:<port>]` for a board on a network. lamella_list_devices lists the boards attached here and the target to give for each.

references.description: The libraries the program uses besides the corlib, each named as its assembly is named, such as "System.Device.Gpio". The corlib is implicit; every other library is a separate reference, as a .NET project names one. The tool's description lists the libraries this server can reference.

tools.name: lamella_deploy
tools.title: Deploy to board (persistent)
tools.description: Compile a C# program, bake it and store it in a board's FLASH over Lamella Link, so the board runs it at every reset: what `lamella deploy <file> --device <d>` does. This OVERWRITES the program the board stores; a board that already stores exactly this program is sent nothing. With `run` (the default) the board then starts it from a reset; lamella_run_on_device starts it and answers with what it prints. A C# program binds against the corlib, which is implicit, and against the libraries it names in `references`: every other library, System.Device.Gpio among them, is a separate reference, as in a .NET project. A program using a library it does not name is refused before the board is opened, naming the library to add. The answer names each assembly the image carries, which build of it, and how much code it puts in the image. The image is built for the board that answers: it carries that board's bus table, and binds its chip family's build of a library built per family, such as System.Device.Gpio with the family's bus drivers.

target.description: Where the board is: `usb`, `usb:<serial>` or `usb:<vid>:<pid>[:<serial>]` for a board's own USB, a serial port such as `COM9`, or `tcp:<host>[:<port>]` for a board on a network. lamella_list_devices lists the boards attached here and the target to give for each.

references.description: The libraries the program uses besides the corlib, each named as its assembly is named, such as "System.Device.Gpio". The corlib is implicit; every other library is a separate reference, as a .NET project names one. The tool's description lists the libraries this server can reference.

run.description: Start the program once it is stored, from a reset, as the board starts it at power-up. With false it starts at the board's next reset.

tools.name: lamella_deploy_status
tools.title: Resident image status
tools.description: Ask a board whether it stores a deployed image: the image's content checksum when it holds one it has verified, or that it holds none. It writes nothing to the board, though its HELLO takes the board back from a program it is running, as every tool that connects to a board does. lamella_deploy and lamella_run_on_device already send nothing to a board that stores exactly the image they build.

target.description: Where the board is: `usb`, `usb:<serial>` or `usb:<vid>:<pid>[:<serial>]` for a board's own USB, a serial port such as `COM9`, or `tcp:<host>[:<port>]` for a board on a network. lamella_list_devices lists the boards attached here and the target to give for each.

tools.name: lamella_flash
tools.title: Flash a board's chip
tools.description: Write an image that ALREADY EXISTS to a board's chip, over a probe or its bootloader volume. ERASES the board's flash: whatever was on it is gone, including another program you did not put there. Takes a path to a built image (.bin/.hex/.elf/.s19, or .uf2 for a volume route), never source -- build one with the `lamella build` verb. A .lmli from lamella_bake is not a chip image: it is what lamella_deploy sends to a board that is already running Lamella. The board is NEVER inferred and an ambiguous bench is REFUSED rather than guessed at: if more than one candidate matches, this returns the candidates and writes nothing, and you must call again naming one. A write to the wrong board succeeds and reports success, which is why. If a sidecar sits beside the image (<image>.manifest.json), it is CHECKED: a board that disagrees with `board`, or bytes that do not hash to what it records, refuse the call before any probe is opened. It is never used to infer `board`. A sidecar that is present and will not parse also refuses -- a claim nobody can check is worse than no claim.

image.description: Path to a built image. Never source.

board.description: Board id, as lamella_boards lists it. Required; never inferred.

via.description: Which mechanism. Omit for the board's own: a debugger soldered to it, or its bootloader drive. `probe` means an EXTERNAL SWD probe and reads every byte back; `volume` cannot read the flash back at all.

probe.description: Probe serial, on a probe route. REQUIRED when more than one probe is attached -- the call is refused until one is named.

volume.description: Bootloader drive, on a volume route. Required when more than one board is in its bootloader.

device.description: System bootloader serial, on a USB DFU route. Required when more than one bootloader is attached.

tools.name: lamella_debug_launch
tools.title: Debug: launch session
tools.description: Start a SOURCE-LEVEL debug session on a board: deploy the program, attach, and stop at entry. Returns a session id (pass it to the other debug tools) and the initial stop (reason + source location). Overwrites the resident image. A C# program binds against the corlib, which is implicit, and against the libraries it names in `references`: every other library, System.Device.Gpio among them, is a separate reference, as in a .NET project. A program using a library it does not name is refused, naming the library to add. The answer names each assembly the image carries, which build of it, and how much code it puts in the image. The image is built for the board that answers: it carries that board's bus table, and binds its chip family's build of a library built per family, such as System.Device.Gpio with the family's bus drivers.

references.description: The libraries the program uses besides the corlib, each named as its assembly is named, such as "System.Device.Gpio". The corlib is implicit; every other library is a separate reference, as a .NET project names one. The tool's description lists the libraries this server can reference.

tools.name: lamella_debug_set_breakpoints
tools.title: Debug: set breakpoints
tools.description: Set source-line breakpoints for the session (replaces the prior set). Returns which requested lines actually bound to code. Can be called mid-session to rebind.

source.description: Optional source file basename; defaults to the launched program.

tools.name: lamella_debug_continue
tools.title: Debug: continue
tools.description: Resume the session until the next breakpoint, an exit, or a fault. Returns the stop (reason, source location, exit code / fault message). It waits at most 20 seconds for the stop, and says so when the program is still running then.

tools.name: lamella_debug_step
tools.title: Debug: step
tools.description: Single-step the session at source granularity: 'in' (step into calls), 'over' (step over), or 'out' (run to return). Returns the new stop location. It waits at most 20 seconds for the stop, and says so when the program is still running then.

tools.name: lamella_debug_stack
tools.title: Debug: stack trace
tools.description: Return the current call stack of the session -- each frame's qualified method name and source location. Read-only.

tools.name: lamella_debug_locals
tools.title: Debug: locals
tools.description: Return the local variables (and arguments) in scope at a stack frame, by name and value. Read-only. Reports that no locals are available on a target that does not supply them.

tools.name: lamella_debug_eval
tools.title: Debug: evaluate
tools.description: Read one variable of the paused session by name -- a local or an argument of a stack frame -- as a debugger's Watch row reads it, and return its value and type. Only a single name is read: anything longer is refused, because nothing that could evaluate it can see the paused frame. It runs no code on the board.

tools.name: lamella_debug_disconnect
tools.title: Debug: disconnect
tools.description: End the debug session and release the board.
